text: Fremont was stitched together in 1956 out of five separate towns: Centerville, Irvington, Mission San José, Niles and Warm Springs.
The city is named for John C. Frémont, who never lived in it.
Mission San José was founded in 1797, the fourteenth of California's twenty-one missions.
Charlie Chaplin filmed The Tramp in Niles in 1915. The character that made him famous was made here.
Essanay Studios shot roughly 250 films in Niles between 1912 and 1916 — westerns, comedies and five Chaplins.
source: Museum of Local History — Movies in Niles

text: Broncho Billy Anderson brought 52 people to Niles in 1912, having picked the town for its weather and its canyon.
The pole at the top of Mission Peak is known as the Mission Peeker. Lining up to be photographed beside it is a local rite.
The peak you can see from most of Fremont is on the city's own logo.
The car plant on the west side was NUMMI before it was Tesla — a joint venture between General Motors and Toyota that ran from 1984 to 2010.
Fremont has been building cars since 1962, when General Motors opened an assembly plant on what had been farmland.
The first transcontinental railroad ran west through Niles Canyon. A heritage line still runs the same track.
The Hayward Fault runs along Fremont's eastern edge, and creeps slowly enough that you can find curbs it has bent.
The Ohlone lived here for thousands of years before the mission was built. Ohlone College is named for them.
Fremont has one of the largest Afghan communities in the United States, concentrated along a stretch of Fremont Boulevard.
The Dumbarton Bridge, opened in 1927, was the first highway bridge built across San Francisco Bay.
Ardenwood is a working farm the city runs as a park — horses in harness and a Victorian house in the middle of it.
source: City of Fremont — Ardenwood Historic Farm

text: Fremont is one of the largest cities in the Bay Area by land area, which is what happens when you incorporate five towns at once.
The Mission San José church you can visit is a reconstruction. The 1797 adobe was brought down by an earthquake in 1868 and rebuilt in the 1980s.
Before 1906, the earthquake Californians meant when they said 'the big one' was the 1868 Hayward quake — and its fault runs through Fremont.
Niles holds an antique flea market that takes over the whole of the boulevard, and has done for decades.
The Shinn family planted a nursery here in the 1850s; the house and its grounds are now a public park.
source: City of Fremont — Shinn Historic Park

text: The five towns each kept their own high school, which is why a city this size has schools named for places most residents cannot point to.
Warm Springs is named for actual warm springs. They fed a resort and later a brewery.
Lake Elizabeth was dug, not found. It was built as the centerpiece of Central Park in the 1960s.
BART reached Fremont in 1972 and stopped there for forty-two years — it was the end of the line until Warm Springs opened in 2017.
The olive trees around Mission San José are descendants of the mission orchard, which is roughly two centuries of the same planting.
Niles is named after a judge, Addison Niles, who sat on the California Supreme Court.
Niles Canyon is narrow enough that the road, the creek and the railway have to take turns.
Alameda Creek drains a watershed of nearly 700 square miles, most of it well east of here, and empties into the Bay at Fremont.
Irvington was called Washington Corners until the 1880s, when a second Washington in the state forced the change.
Centerville's depot still stands. The town grew around the railway rather than the other way round.
The walk up Mission Peak climbs about 2,000 feet in three miles, which is why it is busier at dawn than at noon.
The colored ponds along Fremont's bay edge are salt evaporation ponds. The colors come from what can survive the brine.
source: Don Edwards San Francisco Bay National Wildlife Refuge

text: The refuge on Fremont's bay shore was the first urban National Wildlife Refuge in the United States, established in 1972.
source: Don Edwards San Francisco Bay National Wildlife Refuge

text: The Victorian at Ardenwood was the Patterson family's, and they farmed the land around it for three generations.
source: City of Fremont — Ardenwood Historic Farm

text: The cemetery at Mission San José holds thousands of Ohlone graves, most of them unmarked.
Niles was a railway junction before it was a film town — which is exactly why the film people could get there.
The Fremont plant is one of the largest buildings in the world by floor area, and has been since it was General Motors'.
Fremont built its civic center on empty land between the five old towns so that none of them could claim it.
Adobe is mud, straw and time. The mission was built from the ground it stands on.
